content:
**Nobel Prize in Physics (2010 – 2015)**  

| Year | Laureates | Brief description of the work that earned the prize |
|------|-----------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **2010** | **Andre Geïm** (Netherlands) & **Konstantin Novoselov** (UK) | For **the groundbreaking experiments that led to the isolation of a single layer of carbon atoms – graphene** – and for demonstrating its extraordinary electronic, mechanical and thermal properties. Their work opened a new field of research in two‑dimensional materials. |
| **2011** | **Saul Perlmutter** (USA), **Brian P. Schmidt** (USA) & **Adam G. Riess** (USA) | For the **discovery that the expansion of the Universe is accelerating**. Using observations of distant Type Ia supernovae, they provided the first solid evidence for dark energy, fundamentally changing cosmology. |
| **2012** | **Serge Haroche** (France) & **David J. Wineland** (USA) | For **ground‑breaking experimental methods that manipulate quantum systems**. Haroche developed techniques for trapping and measuring photons without destroying them; Wineland pioneered the control of individual ions, enabling precise quantum logic operations. Their work laid the experimental foundation for quantum information science. |
| **2013** | **François Englert** (Belgium) & **Peter Higgs** (UK) | For the **theoretical discovery of a mechanism that gives mass to elementary particles** (the Higgs mechanism) and the prediction of the Higgs boson, which was confirmed experimentally in 2012 at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. |
| **2014** | **Isamu Akasaki** (Japan), **Hiroshi Amano** (Japan) & **Shuji Nakamura** (USA/Japan) | For the **invention of efficient blue light‑emitting diodes (LEDs)**, which made possible bright, energy‑saving white light sources and displays. Their work transformed lighting technology and reduced global energy consumption. |
| **2015** | **Takaaki Kajita** (Japan) & **Arthur B. McDonald** (Canada) | For the **discovery of neutrino oscillations**, which showed that neutrinos have mass. This breakthrough resolved the solar‑neutrino problem and opened a new window onto particle physics and astrophysics. |

These laureates and their contributions collectively span a remarkable range of physics: from the manipulation of quantum systems and the fundamental origins of particle mass, to cosmology, materials science, and practical applications that impact everyday life.
